title: Integrated Metabolomics and Proteomics Analysis Reveals the Mechanisms of Banxia-Xiexin Decoction in Colitis-Associated Colorectal Cancer
projectDescription: Colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CAC), a subtype of colorectal cancer arising from chronic colonic inflammation, remains without specific therapeutic agents. Banxia-Xiexin decoction (BXD), a traditional Chinese medicine, is clinically used to treat gastritis and ulcerative colitis; however, its efficacy in CAC and associated mechanisms are not well understood. This study aimed to evaluate the therapeutic potential of BXD against CAC and explore its molecular mechanisms. A CAC mouse model was induced using azoxymethane/dextran sulfate sodium (AOM/DSS), and BXD was administered at vary-ing doses (0.95, 1.9, or 3.8 g/kg/day), alongside a sulfasalazine control. Therapeutic effica-cy was assessed by analyzing disease activity index, inflammatory markers, and histo-pathological changes. Additionally, 4D label-free proteomics and serum metabolomics were conducted to elucidate potential mechanisms. BXD significantly improved disease outcomes in CAC mice by reducing colonic inflammation and tumor hyperplasia, while lowering serum levels of TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β, and IFN-γ. Metabolomic profiling suggested that BXD modulates valine, leucine, and isoleucine metabolism. Proteomic analysis re-vealed differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) enriched in complement and coagulation cascade pathways. Key DEPs (Fgg, Fgb, C3, and Cfh) were reversed by BXD treatment, which was confirmed at the mRNA level by qRT-PCR. In conclusion, BXD exerts protec-tive effects against CAC by regulating inflammatory responses and modulating amino acid metabolism and complement pathways. These findings provide novel insights into the pharmacological basis of BXD and support its potential clinical application in CAC therapy.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Samples were ground in liquid nitrogen, suspended in precooled 10% TCA/acetone (1:4, v/v), and precipitated at –20°C for 4 h, then washed thrice with cold acetone. The precipitate was lysed with buffer (8 M urea, 1% protease inhibitor cocktail) and sonicated on ice. For PTM experiments, 3 μM TSA and 50 mM NAM (acetylation), and 1% phosphatase inhibitor (phosphorylation) were included. Debris was removed by centrifugation (12,000 × g, 10 min, 4°C) and protein concentration measured by BCA assay. A protein sample was first combined with an equal volume of chilled acetone and briefly vortexed. Subsequently, four additional volumes of cold acetone were added, and the mixture was allowed to precipitate at -20°C for two hours. The resulting pellet was washed two to three times using ice-cold acetone. Afterwards, the proteins were dissolved in 200 mM TEAB, and dispersed by ultrasonication. Trypsin was introduced at a mass ratio of 1:50 (enzyme to protein) for the initial overnight digestion step. Reduction was performed with 5 mM dithiothreitol at 56°C for half an hour, followed by alkylation using 11 mM iodoacetamide in the dark at room temperature for 15 minutes. Peptide desalting was carried out with a Strata X solid-phase extraction (SPE) column. For LC-MS/MS analysis, the digested peptides were reconstituted in solvent A and then loaded onto a custom-packed reversed-phase column (25 cm length, 100 μm internal diameter). The chromatographic separation employed a binary solvent system: solvent A contained 0.1% formic acid and 2% acetonitrile in water, while solvent B was 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile. The separation was performed on a NanoElute UHPLC platform (Bruker Daltonics) at a constant flow of 500 nL/min, with the following gradient: 6–24% B over 0–14 minutes, 24–35% B from 14–16 minutes, 35–80% B for 16–18 minutes, and 80% B for 18–20 minutes. Peptide ions were introduced via a capillary source and detected using a timsTOF Pro 2 mass spectrometer. The applied electrospray voltage was set to 1.75 kV. Analysis of precursor and fragment ions was carried out with a time-of-flight (TOF) detector. Data acquisition was performed in data-independent parallel accumulation serial fragmentation (dia-PASEF) mode. MS scans covered an m/z range of 300–1,500, with 20 MS/MS (PASEF) scans per cycle (MS/MS range: 400–850; isolation window: 7 m/z). Analysis of the DIA data was performed using the DIA-NN software package (version 1.8). The resulting tandem mass spectra were searched against the Mus_musculus_10090_SP_20230103 FASTA database, which comprises 17,132 protein sequences, along with a reverse decoy database for validation. To ensure high confidence in protein identification, a false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of less than 1% was applied.
dataProcessingProtocol: Protein Function Enrichment  GO Enrichment Analysis   Protein GO annotations are divided into three major categories: biological processes, cellular components, and molecular functions. Fisher's exact test was used to perform GO enrichment significance analysis on differentially expressed proteins (using the identified proteins as background), with P values < 0.05 considered significant.  KEGG pathway enrichment analysis   The Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database was used for pathway enrichment analysis of differentially expressed proteins. Fisher’s exact test was used to perform pathway enrichment significance analysis on differentially expressed proteins (with the identified proteins as the background), and a P value < 0.05 was considered significant.
